_about: Levlofit supplement reference (owner request 2026-11-12). General information from the sources named on each entry, not a prescription: amounts are the official reference intakes and upper limits for healthy adults, not doses Levlofit sets. The app (app/assets/supplements.json, a copy checked by test) uses it for timing on the Diet tab; coach-chat uses it as context. Not reviewed by a clinician.

timings.fat_meal: With a main meal that has some fat (lunch or dinner)
timings.any_meal: With any meal, at the same time each day
timings.evening: With dinner or in the evening
timings.empty: On an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
timings.during: During long or hot sessions, and after them

items.name: Vitamin D3
items.what: Helps the body absorb calcium and keeps bones and muscles working. Low levels are common in India despite sunshine, from indoor life, covered skin and darker skin.
items.when: With your biggest meal that has some fat (it is fat-soluble, so it absorbs better with food). Same time daily or as your doctor prescribes for weekly doses.
items.reference: Reference intake 600 IU (15 mcg) a day for adults to 70 (ICMR-NIN 2020, NIH). Upper limit 4,000 IU (100 mcg) a day unless a doctor prescribes more for a measured deficiency.
items.caution: Get a blood test (25-OH vitamin D) before high doses. Too much over months raises blood calcium. Check with a doctor if you have kidney disease, kidney stones or take heart or diuretic medicines.
items.who: People with little midday sun on bare skin, a measured low level, older adults.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin D fact sheet for health professionals
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020

items.name: Vitamin B12
items.what: Needed for red blood cells and nerves. Found almost only in animal foods, so vegetarians and vegans in India are often low; milk and curd give some.
items.when: Once a day, any time; with breakfast is easy to remember. Absorbs with or without food.
items.reference: Reference intake 2.2 to 2.5 mcg a day for adults (ICMR-NIN 2020; NIH 2.4 mcg). No upper limit set; supplements often carry 500 to 1,000 mcg because only a small share is absorbed.
items.caution: Metformin and acid-reducing medicines (PPIs) lower B12 over time: tell your doctor. Tingling, numbness or tiredness need a blood test, not just a supplement.
items.who: Vegetarians and vegans, people over 50, people on metformin or long-term acid reducers.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin B12 fact sheet
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020

items.name: Omega-3 (fish or algal oil)
items.what: EPA and DHA are fats used in the heart, brain and eyes. People who rarely eat oily fish get little; vegetarians can use algal oil, which has DHA and EPA.
items.when: With a meal (better absorbed and fewer fishy burps). Splitting a larger amount between two meals also helps.
items.reference: Most capsules give 250 to 1,000 mg EPA plus DHA. Up to 5 g a day of EPA plus DHA from supplements is considered safe (US FDA, EFSA). Flaxseed oil gives ALA, which the body turns into very little EPA or DHA.
items.caution: Talk to your doctor first if you take blood thinners or have a bleeding disorder or surgery coming up.
items.who: People who eat oily fish less than twice a week, including vegetarians (algal oil).
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Omega-3 fatty acids fact sheet
EFSA Scientific Opinion on the Tolerable Upper Intake Level of EPA, DHA and DPA, 2012

items.name: Creatine monohydrate
items.what: The best-studied supplement for strength and power: more reps in hard sets and, over weeks, more strength and muscle when you train.
items.when: Every day, training or not, at any time; with a meal or your post-workout shake is easy. Consistency matters, not timing.
items.reference: 3 to 5 g a day; a loading phase is optional (ISSN 2017). Water weight of 1 to 2 kg in the first weeks is normal.
items.caution: Not with kidney disease unless your doctor agrees. Buy plain creatine monohydrate from a tested brand.
items.who: Anyone training for strength, muscle or power; vegetarians often respond well.
sources: Kreider et al., ISSN position stand: creatine, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017

items.name: Whey or plant protein powder
items.what: A convenient protein food, not a must. Useful when meals fall short of your protein target.
items.when: After training, or at the meal where your protein is lowest. Total daily protein matters more than timing.
items.reference: One scoop is usually 20 to 30 g protein; your plan counts it in the day's protein (ISSN 2017: 1.4 to 2.0 g protein per kg a day for most people who train).
items.caution: With kidney disease, ask your doctor. Choose third-party tested products; check the label for added sugar.
items.who: People who cannot reach their protein target from food.
sources: Jager et al., ISSN position stand: protein and exercise, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017

items.name: Caffeine (coffee or pre-workout)
items.what: Improves endurance, strength and focus for many people.
items.when: 30 to 60 minutes before training. Avoid within about 6 hours of bedtime: it cuts sleep.
items.reference: 3 to 6 mg per kg body weight works for most (ISSN 2021). Healthy adults: up to 400 mg a day in total from all sources (EFSA). A cup of filter coffee has roughly 80 to 120 mg.
items.caution: Not in pregnancy above 200 mg a day, or with heart rhythm problems, high blood pressure or anxiety without a doctor's advice. Pre-workout powders may stack several stimulants; read the label.
items.who: People who tolerate caffeine and train hard or long.
sources: Guest et al., ISSN position stand: caffeine and exercise performance, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2021
EFSA Scientific Opinion on the safety of caffeine, 2015

items.name: Magnesium
items.what: Used in muscle and nerve function and energy production. Whole grains, nuts, seeds, dal and leafy greens are good sources.
items.when: With dinner or in the evening; with food it upsets the stomach less.
items.reference: Reference intake about 400 to 420 mg for men and 310 to 320 mg for women a day from all sources (NIH). Upper limit from supplements 350 mg a day; more causes loose stools.
items.caution: Not with kidney disease unless a doctor agrees. Keep 2 hours away from some antibiotics and thyroid medicine.
items.who: People who eat few whole grains, nuts or greens.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Magnesium fact sheet

items.name: Zinc
items.what: Needed for immunity, healing and many enzymes.
items.when: With a meal if it makes you nauseous; keep it 2 hours away from iron or calcium supplements.
items.reference: Reference intake 11 mg (men) and 8 mg (women) a day (NIH; ICMR-NIN 2020 gives 17 and 13 mg for Indian diets high in phytate). Upper limit 40 mg a day.
items.caution: Long use above the upper limit causes copper deficiency.
items.who: Vegetarians and vegans with low intake; only if your diet or a doctor says so.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Zinc fact sheet
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020

items.name: Iron
items.what: Carries oxygen in the blood. Anaemia is common in India, especially in women, and it lowers endurance.
items.when: On an empty stomach with water or something with vitamin C (lemon, amla, orange); keep tea, coffee, milk and calcium 2 hours away. With food if it upsets your stomach.
items.reference: Reference intake about 19 mg (men) and 29 mg (women) a day for Indian diets (ICMR-NIN 2020). Upper limit 45 mg a day without medical advice (NIH).
items.caution: Take iron only after a blood test or on a doctor's advice: too much is harmful. Keep away from children.
items.who: People with a measured low iron or anaemia; often women with heavy periods.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Iron fact sheet
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020

items.name: Calcium
items.what: Builds and keeps bones. Milk, curd, paneer, ragi and sesame are rich sources.
items.when: With a meal (calcium carbonate needs food; citrate works either way), no more than 500 mg at once; 2 hours away from iron or zinc.
items.reference: Reference intake 1,000 mg a day for adults (ICMR-NIN 2020; NIH 1,000 to 1,200 mg). Upper limit 2,500 mg a day for adults to 50 from food and supplements.
items.caution: Count dairy first; many people do not need a tablet. Too much raises the risk of kidney stones.
items.who: People who eat little dairy, ragi or other calcium foods.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Calcium fact sheet
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020

items.name: Multivitamin
items.what: A broad top-up; it does not replace a varied diet and gives little benefit to people who already eat well.
items.when: With breakfast or lunch (the fat-soluble vitamins in it absorb better with food).
items.reference: Choose one near 100% of reference intakes, not megadoses.
items.caution: Add up vitamin D, iron and zinc with any single supplements you take so you stay under the upper limits.
items.who: People with a very limited diet.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Multivitamin/mineral supplements fact sheet

items.name: Electrolytes (ORS or electrolyte drink)
items.what: Replaces the sodium (and some potassium) lost in sweat, which water alone does not.
items.when: During sessions longer than about an hour or in hot, humid weather, and after them. Not needed for short sessions.
items.reference: Sweat losses vary widely; ORS sachets are made to WHO's formula. Sports drinks also carry sugar.
items.caution: With high blood pressure, heart or kidney disease, ask your doctor before adding salt.
items.who: People training long or in Indian summer heat, heavy sweaters.
sources: Sawka et al., ACSM position stand: exercise and fluid replacement, Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007

items.name: Beta-alanine
items.what: Raises muscle carnosine, which helps in hard efforts of about 1 to 4 minutes.
items.when: Every day, split into 2 to 4 smaller doses with meals to reduce the harmless tingling.
items.reference: 4 to 6 g a day for at least 2 to 4 weeks (ISSN 2015).
items.caution: Tingling skin (paraesthesia) is common and harmless; smaller split doses reduce it.
items.who: People doing intervals, HYROX, combat sports or high-rep work.
sources: Trexler et al., ISSN position stand: beta-alanine, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2015

items.name: Citrulline malate
items.what: May add a few reps in high-rep sets; results across studies are mixed.
items.when: About 60 minutes before training.
items.reference: Studies use 6 to 8 g citrulline malate.
items.caution: Usually well tolerated; can upset the stomach.
items.who: Optional; not needed.
sources: Trexler et al., Effects of citrulline supplementation on exercise performance: a meta-analysis, Sports Med 2019

items.name: BCAAs
items.what: Three amino acids already present in protein foods. When daily protein is enough they add little.
items.when: If used at all, around training; reaching your protein target from food or a shake is the better choice.
items.reference: No reference intake; protein foods supply them.
items.caution: Money is better spent on food protein.
items.who: Rarely useful when protein intake is adequate.
sources: Jager et al., ISSN position stand: protein and exercise, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017

items.name: Ashwagandha
items.what: A herb studied for stress, sleep and small strength gains; studies are small and short.
items.when: With dinner or in the evening, as the label says.
items.reference: Studies commonly use 300 to 600 mg of root extract a day for up to 8 to 12 weeks.
items.caution: Not in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Avoid with thyroid disease, autoimmune disease or sedatives unless a doctor agrees; rare liver injury has been reported.
items.who: Optional; ask your doctor if you take any medicine.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Ashwagandha fact sheet for health professionals

items.name: Vitamin C
items.what: An antioxidant needed for collagen and immunity; easy to get from amla, guava, citrus and tomatoes.
items.when: With a meal; with an iron-rich meal it helps absorb plant iron.
items.reference: Reference intake 80 mg (men) and 65 mg (women) a day (ICMR-NIN 2020). Upper limit 2,000 mg a day (NIH).
items.caution: Very high doses cause stomach upset and, in some people, kidney stones.
items.who: People eating little fruit or vegetables.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin C fact sheet
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020

items.name: Collagen
items.what: A protein low in some essential amino acids; studied for tendons and joints with mixed results.
items.when: If used, about 30 to 60 minutes before a session that loads tendons, with some vitamin C.
items.reference: Studies use 10 to 15 g with about 50 mg vitamin C.
items.caution: Does not count fully toward your protein target as a complete protein.
items.who: Optional, for tendon rehab under a physiotherapist.
sources: Shaw et al., Vitamin C-enriched gelatin supplementation before intermittent activity augments collagen synthesis, Am J Clin Nutr 2017

items.name: Probiotic
items.what: Live bacteria; benefits depend on the strain and the reason. Curd and buttermilk are everyday sources.
items.when: With a meal or just before it, as the label says.
items.reference: Doses are counted in CFU and differ by product.
items.caution: Ask a doctor if you have a weakened immune system.
items.who: Optional; a specific reason (for example after antibiotics) matters.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Probiotics fact sheet

items.name: Folic acid (vitamin B9)
items.what: Needed to make new cells; essential before and in early pregnancy. Dal, leafy greens and citrus are good sources.
items.when: Once a day with breakfast.
items.reference: Reference intake about 300 mcg a day for adults, 570 mcg in pregnancy (ICMR-NIN 2020). Upper limit 1,000 mcg a day from supplements and fortified food (NIH).
items.caution: High folic acid can hide a B12 deficiency: check B12 too.
items.who: Anyone planning pregnancy or pregnant (on medical advice), very limited diets.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Folate fact sheet
ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020
